propositions.text: The respondent, Gisèle Gatien, is a career public servant with over 35 years of service, managing a team of 12 in 2011.
propositions.quote: The respondent, Gisèle Gatien, is a career public servant who provided over thirty-five years of service to the country. In 2011, Ms. Gatien held the position of Manager, Federal Workers’ Compensation Program, Ontario Region, in the Department of Human Resources and Skills Development Canada, where she managed a team of 12 subordinates.

paragraphs.summary: The court states Ms. Gatien is a career public servant with over 35 years' service and managed 12 subordinates in 2011.

propositions.text: One subordinate was extremely difficult and transferred due to bullying; Ms. Gatien alleges this employee assaulted her before transfer.
propositions.quote: One of Ms. Gatien’s subordinates appears to have been an extremely difficult employee. This employee was transferred from Ms. Gatien’s unit due to the employee’s inappropriate workplace behaviours, which were eventually determined to have included bullying of co-workers. Ms. Gatien claims that, the day before she was transferred, the employee in question assaulted Ms. Gatien by pulling Ms. Gatien’s hair and hitting her over the head.

paragraphs.summary: The court states a subordinate was difficult, transferred for bullying, and allegedly assaulted Ms. Gatien before transfer.

propositions.text: After transfer, the employee was allowed after-hours access to collect belongings, with union and labour reps present.
propositions.quote: Following the employee’s transfer from the unit, arrangements were made with a departmental labour relations representative to allow the employee back into the workplace after hours to collect her belongings, accompanied by her union representative and a labour relations advisor.

propositions.text: Ms. Gatien was advised of the plan and became stressed, erecting barricades in the workplace directing to the employee's station.
propositions.quote: Ms. Gatien, as the unit manager, was advised of the plan to allow the employee after-hours access to the work site to collect her things. Ms. Gatien became very stressed by the prospect of the employee’s return and erected physical barricades in the workplace, taping filing cabinets shut and cardboard boxes together to build a wall that she papered with arrows to show the way to the employee’s work station.

propositions.text: The union and employee were upset; senior management confronted Ms. Gatien, who apologized in an email.
propositions.quote: The union representative and the employee were upset by the barricades, and senior management confronted Ms. Gatien about them. In an email sent a few days after her superiors questioned her about the barricading incident, Ms. Gatien acknowledged that she ought not have erected the barricades and apologized for her conduct.

paragraphs.summary: The court states Ms. Gatien was advised of after-hours access, became stressed, erected barricades, was confronted, and apologized.

propositions.text: The employer disciplined Ms. Gatien with a 10-day suspension; she was diagnosed with PTSD and took sick leave, never returning full-time.
propositions.quote: The employer decided to discipline Ms. Gatien for her actions and levied a 10 day suspension. Ms. Gatien ended up being diagnosed with post-traumatic stress disorder, was required to take sick leave and did not ever return to work on a full-time basis following the imposition of the 10 day suspension.

paragraphs.summary: The court states Ms. Gatien was suspended 10 days, diagnosed with PTSD, took sick leave, and never returned full-time.

propositions.text: Ms. Gatien filed a grievance seeking to rescind suspension, replace it with reprimand, and $100,000 bad faith damages.
propositions.quote: Ms. Gatien filed a grievance under paragraph 208(1)(b) of the Public Service Labour Relations Act, S.C. 2003, c. 22, s. 2 in which she sought to have the suspension rescinded and replaced with an oral reprimand. In her grievance, Ms. Gatien also requested an award of $100,000.00 as bad faith damages for what she claimed was the unduly insensitive way in which the employer handled the situation.

paragraphs.summary: The court states Ms. Gatien filed a grievance seeking suspension rescinded, oral reprimand, and $100,000 bad faith damages.

propositions.text: The grievance was heard by Vice-Chair Potter who partially allowed it, substituting reprimand for suspension but denied bad faith damages.
propositions.quote: Ms. Gatien referred her grievance to the Public Service Labour Relations Board [PSLRB] for adjudication, and Vice-Chair Potter heard the case over the course of four days. In an award issued September 5, 2013 (reported as 2013 PSLRB 101), Adjudicator Potter allowed the grievance in part and substituted an oral reprimand for the 10 day suspension. However, he declined to make an award for aggravated bad faith damages.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the adjudicator partially allowed the grievance, substituting reprimand but denying bad faith damages.

propositions.text: Ms. Gatien applied for judicial review; Federal Court allowed it, finding adjudicator erred on aggravated damages principles and evidence.
propositions.quote: Ms. Gatien filed an application for judicial review of Adjudicator Potter’s award with the Federal Court. In a judgment dated April 27, 2015 (Gatien v. Attorney General of Canada, 2015 FC 543), Justice O’Keefe of the Federal Court allowed Ms. Gatien’s application for judicial review and found that the Adjudicator had erred in delineating the principles applicable to awards of aggravated damages and in his assessment of the evidence.

propositions.text: The Federal Court remitted the grievance to the Adjudicator for re-determination of aggravated bad faith damages entitlement.
propositions.quote: The Federal Court therefore remitted the grievance to the Adjudicator for re-determination of Ms. Gatien’s entitlement to aggravated bad faith damages.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the Federal Court allowed judicial review, found adjudicator erred, and remitted the grievance for re-determination.

propositions.text: The Attorney General appeals, arguing Federal Court erred on aggravated damages principles and evidentiary findings.
propositions.quote: The Attorney General, on behalf of the employer, has appealed the judgment of the Federal Court to this Court. The appellant argues that the Federal Court erred in finding that the Adjudicator improperly enunciated the principles applicable to awards of aggravated damages and that the Federal Court also erred in in its assessment of the Adjudicator’s evidentiary findings.

paragraphs.summary: The appellant argues the Federal Court erred on aggravated damages principles and evidentiary findings in its judgment.

propositions.text: The court agrees with appellant, would allow appeal, set aside Federal Court decision, dismiss judicial review with costs.
propositions.quote: I agree with the appellant on both points and for the reasons that follow would allow the appeal, set aside the decision of the Federal Court and, rendering the decision which the Federal Court should have made, would dismiss Ms. Gatien’s application for judicial review, with costs.

paragraphs.summary: The court agrees with appellant, would allow appeal, set aside Federal Court decision, and dismiss judicial review with costs.

propositions.text: Relevant parts of adjudicator's award are paragraphs 113-125, on aggravated damages principles and evidence analysis.
propositions.quote: The sections of the Adjudicator’s award that are germane to this appeal are those setting out the principles underlying an award of aggravated damages and analyzing the evidence to determine whether such an award ought to have been made in Ms. Gatien’s case (paragraphs 113-125 of the award).

paragraphs.summary: The court states relevant adjudicator award sections are paragraphs 113-125 on aggravated damages principles and evidence.

propositions.text: Common law on aggravated damages in employment arises in wrongful dismissal cases, allowing damages for inappropriate termination conduct.
propositions.quote: To place these issues in context, it is useful to briefly review the common law jurisprudence, which both the Adjudicator and the Federal Court referred to, dealing with awards of aggravated damages in employment cases. This case law arises in the context of wrongful dismissal actions and provides that an employer may be liable for both punitive damages and mental distress or moral damages if the employer carries out a termination in an inappropriate manner.

paragraphs.summary: The court reviews common law on aggravated damages in wrongful dismissal for inappropriate termination conduct.

propositions.text: Punitive damages require independently actionable, harsh, vindictive, reprehensible, malicious conduct deserving punishment.
propositions.quote: More specifically, punitive damages may be awarded if the employer’s conduct is actionable for reasons going beyond its failure to provide the requisite reasonable notice of termination and if the conduct is so objectionable that the court feels it ought to be sanctioned. As noted by the Supreme Court of Canada in Vorvis v. Insurance Corporation of British Columbia, [1989] 1 S.C.R. 1085, [1989] S.C.J. No. 46 (QL) [Vorvis] at 1107-1008, conduct that may give rise to a punitive damages award must be “harsh, vindictive, reprehensible and malicious” and so “extreme in its nature … that by any reasonable standard it is deserving of full condemnation and punishment”.

propositions.text: Vorvis defines punitive damages conduct as harsh, vindictive, reprehensible, malicious, and deserving full condemnation and punishment.
propositions.quote: As noted by the Supreme Court of Canada in Vorvis v. Insurance Corporation of British Columbia, [1989] 1 S.C.R. 1085, [1989] S.C.J. No. 46 (QL) [Vorvis] at 1107-1008, conduct that may give rise to a punitive damages award must be “harsh, vindictive, reprehensible and malicious” and so “extreme in its nature … that by any reasonable standard it is deserving of full condemnation and punishment”.

paragraphs.summary: The court states punitive damages require independently actionable, harsh, vindictive, reprehensible, malicious conduct deserving punishment, citing Vorvis.

propositions.text: Mental distress damages may be awarded without independently actionable conduct if termination breaches duty of good faith and fair dealing.
propositions.quote: Following the decision of the Supreme Court of Canada in Honda Canada Inc. v. Keays, 2008 SCC 39, [2008] 2 S.C.R. 362 [Honda v. Keays], mental distress or moral damages, which are different from punitive damages, may be awarded in the absence of independently actionable employer conduct if a termination is carried out in a manner that breaches the employer’s duty of good faith and fair dealing.

propositions.text: Honda v. Keays holds mental distress damages differ from punitive damages and may be awarded for bad faith termination without separate actionable conduct.
propositions.quote: Following the decision of the Supreme Court of Canada in Honda Canada Inc. v. Keays, 2008 SCC 39, [2008] 2 S.C.R. 362 [Honda v. Keays], mental distress or moral damages, which are different from punitive damages, may be awarded in the absence of independently actionable employer conduct if a termination is carried out in a manner that breaches the employer’s duty of good faith and fair dealing.

paragraphs.summary: The court states Honda v. Keays allows mental distress damages without independently actionable conduct for bad faith termination.

propositions.text: Honda v. Keays examples of mental distress damages include attacking reputation, misrepresentation, or dismissal to deprive rights.
propositions.quote: In Honda v. Keays, Justice Bastarache, writing for the majority, noted at paragraph 59 that examples of conduct that could give rise to mental distress or moral damages might include such things as “attacking the employee’s reputation by declarations made at the time of dismissal, misrepresentation regarding the reason for the decision, or dismissal meant to deprive the employee of a pension benefit or other right, [such as] permanent status”.

paragraphs.summary: The court states Honda v. Keays examples of mental distress damages include reputation attacks, misrepresentation, or dismissal to deprive rights.

propositions.text: Mental distress damages are compensatory under contract law, reflecting distress caused by bad faith dismissal, set by reference to case law.
propositions.quote: According to Honda v. Keays, mental distress or moral damages are awarded under general contractual principles, on the basis that at the time the parties entered into the employment contract they will be deemed to have contemplated that a breach of the duty of good faith and fair dealing would give rise to damages where the unfair or bad faith manner of dismissal causes distress to the terminated employee. Such damages are compensatory and aim to compensate the employee for the distress suffered, with the quantum being set by the court with reference to previously-decided case law and the nature and severity of the distress suffered by the employee.

paragraphs.summary: The court states mental distress damages are compensatory under contract law, reflecting distress from bad faith dismissal, set by case law.

propositions.text: Before Honda v. Keays, aggravated damages required independently actionable employer conduct, as accepted in Wallace and Vorvis.
propositions.quote: Prior to the decision in Honda v. Keays, to give rise to aggravated damages, including moral damages or damages for mental distress, the impugned employer conduct had to be independently actionable. However, in Wallace v. United Grain Growers Ltd., [1997] 3 S.C.R. 701, [1997] S.C.J. No. 94 (QL) [Wallace] and Vorvis, the Supreme Court accepted that a breach of the duty of good faith and fair dealing could constitute independently actionable conduct founding an award of mental distress or moral damages.

paragraphs.summary: The court states before Honda v. Keays, aggravated damages required independently actionable conduct, per Wallace and Vorvis.

propositions.text: Before Honda v. Keays, bad faith discharge damages were calculated by extending notice period, as in Wallace case.
propositions.quote: In addition, prior to the decision of the Supreme Court in Honda v. Keays, damages for bad faith discharge were calculated through an extension of the notice period. In Wallace, the employer had abruptly terminated Mr. Wallace’s employment following 14 years of service and had falsely maintained that the dismissal was for cause until the beginning of the wrongful dismissal trial. These unfounded allegations seriously diminished Mr. Wallace’s prospects for finding similar employment and caused him to suffer from depression. To compensate Mr. Wallace for the employer’s conduct in effecting the dismissal, the Supreme Court extended the notice period to 24 months.

paragraphs.summary: The court states before Honda v. Keays, bad faith discharge damages were calculated by extending notice period, as in Wallace.

propositions.text: Honda v. Keays discarded Wallace approach; damages for bad faith dismissal awarded under Hadley principle, not by extending notice period.
propositions.quote: The approach set out in Wallace, of extending the notice period and of characterizing a breach of the duty of good faith and fair dealing as being independently actionable, was discarded by the Supreme Court in Honda v. Keays. There, Justice Bastarache noted at paragraph 59 that: [t]o be perfectly clear, I will conclude this analysis of our jurisprudence by saying that there is no reason to retain the distinction between “true aggravated damages” resulting from a separate cause of action and moral damages resulting from conduct in the manner of termination. Damages attributable to conduct in the manner of dismissal are always to be awarded under the Hadley principle. Moreover, in cases where damages are awarded, no extension of the notice period is to be used to determine the proper amount to be paid. The amount is to be fixed according to the same principles and in the same way as in all other cases dealing with moral damages. Thus, if the employee can prove that the manner of dismissal caused mental distress that was in the contemplation of the parties, those damages will be awarded not through an arbitrary extension of the notice period, but through an award that reflects the actual damages.

paragraphs.summary: The court states Honda v. Keays discarded Wallace approach; damages awarded under Hadley principle, not by extending notice period.

propositions.text: The Adjudicator accepted that PSLRB could award bad faith damages in a suspension grievance context.
propositions.quote: With this background in mind, it is now possible to turn to the Adjudicator’s award in this case. In delineating the principles applicable to an award for bad faith damages, the Adjudicator implicitly accepted that such damages could be awarded by the PSLRB in the context of a grievance challenging a suspension.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the Adjudicator accepted PSLRB could award bad faith damages in suspension grievance context.

propositions.text: The Adjudicator relied on common law wrongful dismissal cases and discussed Wallace decision on bad faith damages.
propositions.quote: The Adjudicator premised his decision on the common law wrongful dismissal case law that Ms. Gatien relied on, summarized above, and commenced his analysis of the applicable principles by discussing the decision of the Supreme Court of Canada in Wallace.

propositions.text: In Wallace, damages for bad faith discharge require separate actionable conduct causing mental distress.
propositions.quote: The Adjudicator noted that in Wallace the Supreme Court determined that damages for bad faith discharge may only be awarded if “there was a separate actionable course of conduct apart from the issuance of discipline itself that caused mental distress or suffering” (at paragraph 116 of the award).

propositions.text: The Adjudicator found the 10-day suspension was excessive but not a separate actionable course of conduct to allow damages.
propositions.quote: The Adjudicator continued by stating: “[t]he grievor argued that the imposition of the 10-day suspension was unduly harsh and vindictive. While I did agree that it was excessive, given the facts in this case, it cannot lead to damages because it is not a ‘separate actionable course of conduct’” (at paragraph 117 of the award).

paragraphs.summary: The Adjudicator relied on Wallace, found suspension excessive but not separate actionable conduct for damages.

propositions.text: Adjudicator found employer's conduct did not warrant damages award under Honda v. Keays
propositions.quote: The Adjudicator then analyzed the employer’s conduct and found that it did not warrant an award of damages.

propositions.text: Adjudicator held employer's conduct was far removed from behaviours warranting moral damages
propositions.quote: the employer’s conduct in the case before him was “far removed” from the type of behaviours that Justice Bastarache indicated could give rise to an award of moral damages or damages for mental distress.

propositions.text: Adjudicator noted no attack on reputation or intent to deprive pension, discipline was excessive but modified
propositions.quote: [t]he grievor’s reputation was not attacked; nor was there any intent to deprive her of a pension, for example. Management took action with respect to the grievor’s behaviour, which she herself acknowledged was worthy of some discipline. The fact that the discipline imposed was excessive is compensated by modifying the penalty.

paragraphs.summary: The Adjudicator found employer's conduct did not warrant damages, was far removed from conduct in Honda v. Keays, and discipline was excessive but modified.

propositions.text: Adjudicator dismissed claim employer should have known discipline would cause mental suffering
propositions.quote: The Adjudicator also considered and dismissed Ms. Gatien’s claim that the employer should have known that imposing discipline would cause her mental suffering and loss of professional standing.

propositions.text: Adjudicator held employer could not have anticipated distress without medical evidence before suspension
propositions.quote: The Adjudicator held that the employer could not have anticipated that Ms. Gatien would have suffered distress as it had not been provided with any medical evidence about Ms. Gatien’s condition prior to the imposition of the 10 day suspension.

propositions.text: Adjudicator found suspension manner was not egregious or over the top
propositions.quote: the manner in which the suspension was imposed was not “egregious, or over the top, as was the situation in much of the case law reviewed”

paragraphs.summary: The Adjudicator dismissed claim employer should have known of mental suffering, found no medical evidence, and suspension was not egregious.

propositions.text: Adjudicator found no evidence supporting loss of professional standing claim
propositions.quote: As for the alleged loss of professional standing, the Adjudicator found there was no evidence to support this claim

propositions.text: Adjudicator noted award should correct any loss of standing
propositions.quote: noted in any event his award (in which Ms. Gatien was vindicated) should correct any loss of standing that Ms. Gatien might have suffered.

paragraphs.summary: The Adjudicator found no evidence for loss of professional standing and said award should correct any such loss.

propositions.text: Adjudicator denied Ms. Gatien’s request for bad faith damages
propositions.quote: The Adjudicator therefore denied Ms. Gatien’s request for bad faith damages.

paragraphs.summary: The Adjudicator denied Ms. Gatien's request for bad faith damages.

propositions.text: Federal Court held correctness standard applies to legal test portion, reasonableness to application to facts
propositions.quote: the Federal Court held that the correctness standard of review is to be applied to the portion of the Adjudicator’s decision setting out the test for an award of bad faith damages and that the reasonableness standard applies to the Adjudicator’s application of the test to the facts before him.

paragraphs.summary: The Federal Court held correctness standard applies to legal test, reasonableness to application to facts.

propositions.text: Federal Court found Adjudicator erred by requiring independently actionable conduct for bad faith damages
propositions.quote: the Federal Court determined that the Adjudicator had held that bad faith damages could not be awarded in the absence of independently actionable conduct, and that in so holding, the Adjudicator erred because this requirement has been set aside by the Supreme Court of Canada in Honda v. Keays.

paragraphs.summary: The Federal Court found the Adjudicator erred requiring independently actionable conduct for bad faith damages.

propositions.text: Federal Court ruled Adjudicator's award unreasonable; employer had medical info before discipline
propositions.quote: the Federal Court ruled that the Adjudicator’s award was unreasonable because, contrary to what the Adjudicator found, the employer was in possession of medical information about Ms. Gatien prior to the imposition of discipline.

propositions.text: Medical info included supervisor's observation of shock, medical note for sick leave, and stress disclosure
propositions.quote: this information included the fact that Ms. Gatien’s supervisor observed her to have been in shock and tears after the alleged assault, that she had provided a medical note that authorized a brief period of sick leave due to “recent stressors” before she was disciplined and that Ms. Gatien had told her supervisor that she was stressed during an investigative meeting.

paragraphs.summary: The Federal Court ruled the award unreasonable; employer had medical info including shock, sick leave note, and stress disclosure.

propositions.text: One superior suggested Ms. Gatien mismanaged situation; Federal Court found no evidence for this
propositions.quote: one of Ms. Gatien’s superiors suggested in her evidence before the PSLRB that Ms. Gatien had mismanaged the situation with the difficult employee. The Federal Court held at paragraph 53 of its Reasons for Judgment that “the evidence does not show this at all”

propositions.text: Federal Court said improper management attitude should be re-examined for aggravated damages
propositions.quote: this improper attitude on the part of management should be re-examined by the Adjudicator to determine whether an award of aggravated damages should be made.

paragraphs.summary: The Federal Court found no evidence Ms. Gatien mismanaged situation and ordered re-examination of management attitude for aggravated damages.

propositions.text: Court turns to analyze merits of appeal
propositions.quote: Having set out the background to this appeal, I turn now to analyze its merits.

paragraphs.summary: The Court turns to analyze the merits of the appeal.

propositions.text: Court must step into Federal Court's shoes to determine standard of review and its application
propositions.quote: this Court is required to step into the shoes of the Federal Court in order to determine whether it selected the appropriate standard of review and whether it applied that standard correctly

propositions.text: Agraira and MacFarlane establish appellate court's role in reviewing Federal Court's standard of review choice and application
propositions.quote: Agraira v. Canada (Public Safety and Emergency Preparedness), 2013 SCC 36...; MacFarlane v. Day & Ross Inc., 2014 FCA 199

paragraphs.summary: The Court must review whether the Federal Court chose and applied the correct standard of review, per Agraira and MacFarlane.

propositions.text: Federal Court erred in selecting correctness standard for legal test of bad faith damages
propositions.quote: I believe that the Federal Court erred in selecting the correctness standard for the review of the Adjudicator’s determination of the legal test for an award of aggravated bad faith damages.

propositions.text: Reasonableness standard applies to both legal test and application to facts for bad faith damages
propositions.quote: it ought to have applied the reasonableness standard to both the Adjudicator’s enunciation of the legal test for bad faith damages and to the application of the test to the facts of Ms. Gatien’s case

propositions.text: Case law establishes reasonableness standard applies to both questions
propositions.quote: as the case law establishes that the reasonableness standard applies to both questions.

paragraphs.summary: The Court finds Federal Court erred selecting correctness standard; reasonableness applies to legal test and facts application.

propositions.text: Full standard of review analysis not required if previous case law settles applicable standard
propositions.quote: a full-blown standard of review analysis is not required where previous case law has satisfactorily settled the applicable standard of review.

propositions.text: Post-Dunsmuir binding authority settles standard of review in some cases
propositions.quote: One of the circumstances where the previous case law may be said to have satisfactorily settled the applicable standard involves a situation where the issue has been canvassed in binding authority, post-Dunsmuir.

paragraphs.summary: Full standard of review analysis not needed if prior case law settles standard, especially post-Dunsmuir binding authority.

propositions.text: Supreme Court recognizes deference owed to labour adjudicators applying common law in labour context
propositions.quote: adjudicators are owed deference in respect of their application of common or civil law rules in the labour relations context

propositions.text: Deference owed when labour adjudicators craft novel remedies or adapt law to novel facts
propositions.quote: deference is similarly owed when labour adjudicators craft novel remedies or adapt common or civil law rules to novel factual situations.

propositions.text: Nor-Man case holds reasonableness standard applies to labour arbitrators' application of promissory estoppel
propositions.quote: In Nor-Man Regional Health Authority Inc. v. Manitoba Association of Health Care Professionals...the reasonableness standard of review applies to labour arbitrators’ application of the common law doctrine of promissory estoppel.

propositions.text: Labour arbitrators authorized and equipped to adapt legal doctrines within arbitral creativity
propositions.quote: labour arbitrators are authorized by their broad statutory and contractual mandates...to adapt the legal and equitable doctrines they find relevant within the contained sphere of arbitral creativity.

paragraphs.summary: Supreme Court holds labour adjudicators deserve deference applying or adapting common law, per Nor-Man case applying reasonableness standard.

propositions.text: Appellate courts have applied reasonableness standard reviewing labour adjudicators' common law applications
propositions.quote: Following Nor-Man, appellate courts have applied the reasonableness standard in reviewing labour adjudicators’ applications of common law doctrines on several occasions.

paragraphs.summary: Appellate courts have applied reasonableness standard reviewing labour adjudicators' common law applications.

propositions.text: Saskatchewan Court of Appeal applied reasonableness standard in multiple labour law doctrine reviews
propositions.quote: in Viterra Inc. v. Grain Services Union...Canadian Union of Public Employees...United Food and Commercial Workers...

paragraphs.summary: Saskatchewan Court of Appeal applied reasonableness standard reviewing labour law doctrines in multiple cases.

propositions.text: Quebec Court of Appeal endorsed reasonableness standard reviewing Quebec Labour Board's application of Civil Code principle
propositions.quote: in Syndicat des employés de Au Dragon forgé inc. c. Québec...the Quebec Court of Appeal endorsed the reasonableness standard as the appropriate standard for reviewing the Quebec Labour Board’s application of the civilian principle of vitiation of consent

paragraphs.summary: Quebec Court of Appeal endorsed reasonableness standard reviewing Quebec Labour Board's application of Civil Code principle.

propositions.text: New Brunswick Court of Appeal applied reasonableness standard reviewing labour board's application of common law harmonization principle
propositions.quote: in New Brunswick (Department of Natural Resources) v. Pinder...the New Brunswick Court of Appeal applied the reasonableness standard to review a labour board decision that applied the common law “harmonization principle”

paragraphs.summary: New Brunswick Court of Appeal applied reasonableness standard reviewing labour board's application of harmonization principle.

propositions.text: Ontario Court of Appeal applied reasonableness standard reviewing Labour Relations Board's estoppel imposition
propositions.quote: in EllisDon Corp. v. Ontario Sheet Metal Workers' and Roofers' Conference...the Ontario Court of Appeal applied the reasonableness standard in reviewing the Ontario Labour Relations Board’s imposition of a two-year estoppel

paragraphs.summary: Ontario Court of Appeal applied reasonableness standard reviewing Labour Relations Board's estoppel imposition.

propositions.text: Application of common or civil law doctrines intertwined with labour adjudicator expertise merits deference
propositions.quote: application of common or civil law doctrines to workplace issues...are entitled to deference.

propositions.text: Remedial matters are core expertise of labour adjudicators, better suited than courts to assess workplace wrongs
propositions.quote: remedial matters are at the very heart of the specialized expertise of labour adjudicators, who are much better situated than a reviewing court when it comes to assessing whether and how workplace wrongs should be addressed

propositions.text: Heustis and Royal Oak Mines support deference to labour adjudicators on remedies
propositions.quote: see, for example, Heustis v. New Brunswick Electric Power Commission...Royal Oak Mines Inc. v. Canada (Labour Relations Board)

paragraphs.summary: Labour adjudicators deserve deference applying common law doctrines and remedies due to expertise, supported by Heustis and Royal Oak Mines.

propositions.text: Determining compensatory damages for suspension manner is core PSLRB function, not general legal question
propositions.quote: Determining whether compensatory damages should be awarded for the manner in which a suspension was imposed falls squarely within the core function of a PSLRB adjudicator

propositions.text: Such decisions do not subvert legal system even if reviewing court finds error, per Canadian Human Rights Commission case
propositions.quote: a decision on whether such compensation should include particular components...would not “subvert the legal system, even if a reviewing court found it to be in error”

paragraphs.summary: Determining compensatory damages for suspension is core PSLRB function and does not subvert legal system even if error found.

propositions.text: Determination of damages for bad faith employer conduct is specialized expertise of labour adjudicators, not general legal importance.
propositions.quote: determination of when damages may be awarded for bad faith conduct of an employer is not a matter of general importance to the legal system as a whole, but, rather, a matter that falls within the specialized expertise of labour adjudicators.

propositions.text: Federal Court should have applied reasonableness standard to review the Adjudicator’s award.
propositions.quote: The Federal Court therefore should have applied the reasonableness standard to review the entirety of the Adjudicator’s award in this case.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds damages for bad faith employer conduct fall under labour adjudicators' expertise and Federal Court should apply reasonableness standard to review award.

propositions.text: Whether the Adjudicator’s legal test and application for aggravated bad faith damages were reasonable.
propositions.quote: I turn now to consider whether the Adjudicator’s delineation of the legal test for an award of aggravated bad faith damages and his application of the test to the circumstances of Ms. Gatien’s case were reasonable.

propositions.text: The Adjudicator’s legal test and application were reasonable.
propositions.quote: In my view, they were.

paragraphs.summary: The court considers and finds the Adjudicator’s legal test and application for aggravated damages reasonable.

propositions.text: Adjudicator did not require independently actionable conduct as prerequisite for aggravated damages.
propositions.quote: the Adjudicator did not require that there be independently actionable conduct as a pre-requisite to an award of aggravated damages for bad faith employer conduct.

propositions.text: Adjudicator quoted Justice Bastarache’s judgment in Honda v. Keays stating independently actionable conduct not required.
propositions.quote: the Adjudicator quoted at length from Justice Bastarache’s judgment in Honda v. Keays, including the passage where Justice Bastarache noted that independently actionable conduct is not required for an award of aggravated damages.

propositions.text: Adjudicator applied Honda v. Keays test and decided aggravated damages not warranted as employer’s conduct was far removed from cases awarding such damages.
propositions.quote: The Adjudicator then applied the test from Honda v. Keays to Ms. Gatien’s situation and decided aggravated damages were not warranted as the employer’s conduct was “far removed” from the sorts of situations where aggravated bad faith damages had been awarded.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Adjudicator did not require independently actionable conduct and reasonably applied Honda v. Keays to deny aggravated damages.

propositions.text: Adjudicator’s earlier reference to Wallace and independently actionable conduct must be read in light of later reasoning.
propositions.quote: The Adjudicator’s reference to Wallace and to the need for independently actionable conduct appeared much earlier in the award and, in my view, must be read in light of what follows, where the heart of the Adjudicator’s reasoning is set out.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Adjudicator’s earlier references to Wallace must be read in context of his full reasoning.

propositions.text: Distinction between Wallace and Honda v. Keays is not stark; both involve employer conduct beyond reasonable notice breach causing additional damages.
propositions.quote: the distinction between the holdings in Wallace and Honda v. Keays is not as stark as counsel for Ms. Gatien suggests. In both cases, the same type of employer conduct – that went beyond a breach of the duty to provide reasonable notice of termination – gave rise to additional damages.

propositions.text: Wallace called conduct independently actionable extending notice; Honda v. Keays held conduct not independently actionable but gave rise to mental distress damages.
propositions.quote: In Wallace, this conduct was called independently actionable and caused the notice period to be extended, whereas in Honda v. Keays the Supreme Court held the conduct was not independently actionable and would instead give rise to mental distress or moral damages under general contractual principles.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Wallace and Honda v. Keays differ in labeling but both address employer conduct beyond notice breach causing damages.

propositions.text: Adjudicator’s focus on employer conduct nature and contrast with cases awarding aggravated damages is reasonable despite some unclear award portions.
propositions.quote: As the Adjudicator focussed on the nature of the employer’s conduct and contrasted it with the type of conduct that had been found to give rise to aggravated bad faith damages, his treatment of the issue cannot be said to be unreasonable as his reasoning encapsulates the essence of the common law case law, even though portions of the award may not be as clear as they could be.

propositions.text: Adjudicator’s conclusion to decline aggravated damages is reasonable as employer’s conduct was far less objectionable than in cases awarding such damages.
propositions.quote: Nor can his conclusion to decline to award aggravated damages be said to be unreasonable as Ms. Gatien’s case was decidedly different from those where bad faith damages had been awarded, in that the employer’s conduct in her case was far less objectionable.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Adjudicator reasonably contrasted employer conduct and reasonably declined aggravated damages.

propositions.text: Evidence supported Adjudicator’s reasonable conclusion employer was unaware of Ms. Gatien’s mental health condition when imposing discipline.
propositions.quote: there was evidence before the Adjudicator from which he could have reasonably concluded that the employer was unaware of Ms. Gatien’s mental health condition when it imposed discipline.

propositions.text: Ms. Gatien’s tears or stress statements do not prove recognized psychiatric illness.
propositions.quote: The mere fact that she dissolved into tears or said she was stressed falls well short of proof of her suffering from a recognized psychiatric illness.

propositions.text: Physician’s brief note about stressors for sick leave does not communicate PTSD diagnosis to employer.
propositions.quote: the brief note from her physician, which merely referred to recent stressors to support a short period of sick leave falls well short of communicating to the employer that Ms. Gatien was suffering from or was likely to suffer from post-traumatic stress disorder.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds evidence reasonably supports that employer was unaware of Ms. Gatien’s mental health condition when disciplining her.

propositions.text: Stress should not be equated with disability, supported by case law.
propositions.quote: the case law recognizes that one cannot equate stress with a disability: Halfacree v. Canada (Attorney General), 2014 FC 360 at paragraph 37, aff’d 2015 FCA 98 at paragraph 15; Riche v. Treasury Board (Department of National Defence), 2013 PSLRB 35 at paragraphs 130-131; Crowley v. Liquor Control Board of Ontario, 2011 HRTO 1429 at paragraphs 57-63.

propositions.text: Adjudicator had rational basis to conclude employer lacked medical information about Ms. Gatien’s condition when imposing discipline.
propositions.quote: Thus, there was a rational basis for the Adjudicator to conclude that the employer did not have any medical information about Ms. Gatien’s condition at the time it decided to impose discipline.

propositions.text: Federal Court erred in finding Adjudicator’s conclusion unreasonable.
propositions.quote: The Federal Court therefore erred in finding this conclusion to be unreasonable.

paragraphs.summary: The respondent argues stress is not disability; the court finds Adjudicator reasonably concluded employer lacked medical info and Federal Court erred.

propositions.text: Federal Court erred by re-weighing evidence on whether Ms. Gatien mishandled situation with difficult employee.
propositions.quote: The Federal Court also erred in seeking to re-weigh the evidence to determine whether Ms. Gatien had mishandled the situation with the difficult employee and in stating that the “evidence does not show this at all”.

propositions.text: Adjudicator considered Ms. Gatien’s claim that employer’s erroneous belief about her competence led to unwarranted discipline and weighed evidence accordingly.
propositions.quote: The Adjudicator was aware of Ms. Gatien’s suggestion that the employer’s erroneous belief about her competence had led to unwarranted discipline and weighed this claim in light of the evidence.

propositions.text: Adjudicator is charged with hearing witnesses and weighing evidence; Federal Court should not make its own evidentiary conclusions.
propositions.quote: As these factors were considered by the Adjudicator – who was charged with hearing the witnesses and weighing the evidence – it was incorrect for the Federal Court to seek to make its own evidentiary conclusions on the point.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Federal Court erred by re-weighing evidence and should defer to Adjudicator’s findings on employer’s erroneous belief and discipline.

propositions.text: Evidence before PSLRB supported Adjudicator’s conclusion employer’s conduct was not egregious enough for aggravated damages.
propositions.quote: the evidence before the PSLRB amply supported the Adjudicator’s conclusion that the employer’s conduct in this case was not so egregious as to warrant an award of aggravated damages.

propositions.text: Federal Court erred in finding Adjudicator’s evidentiary conclusions unreasonable and in intervening on common law principles treatment.
propositions.quote: Thus, the Federal Court erred in finding the Adjudicator’s evidentiary conclusions to be unreasonable and in finding that the Adjudicator’s treatment of the common law principles warranted intervention.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds evidence supported Adjudicator’s conclusion and Federal Court erred in intervening on evidentiary and legal grounds.

propositions.text: Appeal allowed with costs; Federal Court order set aside; judicial review application dismissed with costs.
propositions.quote: I would allow the appeal with costs, set aside the order of the Federal Court, and rendering the order which the Federal Court should have made, would dismiss the application for judicial review, with costs.

paragraphs.summary: The court allows the appeal, sets aside Federal Court order, and dismisses judicial review application with costs.
